en: From the *General Preface* of the *Compendium of the Supreme Victories of Nanyue*, Volume One:
The record of the Upper Truths states that Zhurong ruled Mount Heng and Mount Huo as the Red Emperor; this is precisely Mount Heng.
Mount Heng is the Southern Peak among the Five Peaks (*wǔyè*), which corresponds to what is referred to in the *Rites of Zhou* (*Zhōu guān*) as the region of Jingzhou.
It is also the Mount Wanwei mentioned in the *Book of Xia*.
According to the Daoist scriptures:
Each of the Five Peaks and Five Mountains has its own reserves of attendants.
In ancient times, when the Yellow Emperor traveled to observe the six realms of the universe,
he summoned the spirits and deities.
One observes that the four peaks of the East, West, North,
and Center all have ministers who assist in the mandate of Heaven;
only the Southern Peak stands alone, without such an official.
Thereupon, together with Changyu, Limu, Fangming, and others, he presented his petition to the Three Heavens.
The Most High commissioned Mount Huo and Mount Qian as the Crown Princes of the Southern Peak,
and invested Mount Qingcheng as the Lord of the Immortals.
He appointed [Hui]lu as a messenger,
ordering him to oversee Mount Heng as a pillar of state;
he was elevated for his virtue and rectitude to serve as the presiding leader.
The Crown Prince is the secondary lord of Mount Heng.
The *Shu yizhi* states that the Southern Peak is the left arm of Pangu.
When Emperor Wu of the Han dynasty went on his southern tour,
because the Southern Peak was too remote,
he relocated its sacrificial rites to Lujiang.
This also accords with the supplementary meaning of Xuanyuan.
The *Xiangzhong ji* states:
"Mount Heng is the numinous terrace of Zhuling."
The Treasure Cave of Great Emptiness receives the energy of the Zhèn (Epsilon Draconis) mansion above;
it weighs virtue and balances all things.
It corresponds to the celestial pole and its axis;
thus it is named Mount Heng.
Below, it rests upon the Palace of Departure.
It encompasses the positions of the Fire Region;
the Red Emperor occupies its ridges,
and Zhurong dwells upon its southern slopes.
Therefore it is called the Southern Peak (Nanyue). The *Yugong* states:
"From Jing to the south of Hengyang is the province of Jing."
It is further stated:
"He toured the south and reached Mount Heng.
Kong's commentary identifies the Southern Peak as Mount Heng. The *Erya* states: [Mount Heng is the Southern Peak].
Mount Huo is the Southern Peak;
it is the same as Mount Heng and Mount Huo.
Furthermore, the *Wuyue jing* (Scripture on the Five Peaks) states:
Mount Lu, Mount Magu, Mount Yusi, Mount Dongyang, Mount Dawei, Mount Jiuyi, Mount Luofu, and other mountains serve as its supporting ministers.
Xu Lingqi’s *Record of the Southern Peak* states:
"The Zhu-ling Grotto-Heaven is named Tai-xu;
it is the heaven of Xiao-you."
It encircles eight hundred li.
Within it are the Jade Altar of Green Jade, the Altar of the Radiant Heaven, the Cave of Mysterious Spirit, and the True Ruins—these four blessed sites.
Huíyàn Peak serves as its head.
Yue-lu serves as its feet.
Furthermore, the *Wu-yue zhen-xing tu* (Diagram of the True Forms of the Five Peaks) states:
"Above it flows vermilion."
It is forty li square and produces *zhī* fungi.
To the south are the Tianjin and Ganquan springs.
By drinking it, one attains longevity and does not die.
To the east are jade sands, *zengqing* (azurite), and white quartz;
to the west is the Kun-water.
To the north is the red fungus (*zhī*).
From its base to its summit,
it measures nine thousand seven hundred and thirty *zhàng*.
To the east it reaches Dongyang;
to the west it abuts Baihe and Yunyang, facing south. Great enclosures crouch to its north, while to the southwest it borders the Xiang River.
From the River Xiang to Changsha is seven hundred li.
To the northeast, it reaches Changsha in two hundred and seventy li;
to the west, it abuts Hengyang at ninety li.
The Stone Drums are the western gate of Zhuling;
Qingcao is the left armpit of Mount Heng.
It is thirty li beyond the county seat.
The cypress and pine trees lining both sides of the path form an unbroken screen of verdant green.
Even in the height of summer, one need not rely on a parasol;
the cool, whistling breeze stirs the ears and eyes with its rustling melody.
The Way has four stations,
serving as resting places for travelers;
such is the topography of that mountain.
Nine orientations and nine aversions correspond to the number of the nine yangs;
its contemplation is boundless.
It is indeed the third of the thirty-six grotto-heavens (*dongtian*).
Thus, Nanyue Zhuling Dongtian Poem by Master Chongmiao Li Sichong says:
Seventy-two peaks rise in jagged tiers at Lingfeng;
Mount Zige and Mount Furong stand in the misty distance.
Their reflections soak into the Xiang and Xiangjiang rivers, winding through the veins of the earth.
The towering peaks support the constellations of Yi and Zhen, piercing the celestial gates;
the Jade Tablet of the True Lord illuminates ten thousand autumns,
while the Vermilion Emperor’s Palace of Jasper guards the eight barbarian tribes.
It is like the Great Chun tree of our Emperor;
the Ten-Thousand-Year Pine stands upon the highest mountain.
It was originally registered in Hengyang.
In the fifth year of the Tianfu era, it was first detached and attached to Changsha Commandery.
During the Chunhua era, Cheng Xun, the Governor of Hengyang,
again requested that it be reattached to Hengyang.
In the fourth year, an imperial edict was finally issued to re-establish its affiliation with Tanzhou,
so as to facilitate the state’s prayers for rain and the people’s payment of taxes;
this followed the petition submitted by the Commissioner for Military Affairs, Lei Youzhong.
The Miraculous Traces of the Five Peaks. Regarding Mount Zhurong among the Miraculous Traces of the Five Peaks:
in ancient times, during the era of Yanhuang, it was the place where Lord Zhurong dwelt and rested.
It was for this reason that it was so named.
Thus, the *Guangji* states:
"This is where Zhurong dwells upon Mount Heng."
The shape of the crown of the head resembles the head of a vermilion bird (zhūjué).
The primal qi ascends and connects [to the heavens].
It is the station governed by the Elder Lord of the Brilliant Star and the Great Sun.
Among these, the one presiding over the summer qi nurtures and grows all things,
causing the spirits of Bing and Ding to exercise the Heavenly Virtue.
He causes the spirits of the hours Ji and Wu to rectify the terrestrial qi.
On the day of the commencement of summer, the myriad spirits always ascend this peak and enter the Crimson Stone Jade Gate.
They paid their respects to the Old Lord of Fire,
received the Celestial Mysterious Talismans,
and each returned to the four directions.
They summon the hundred deities and slay malevolent ghosts;
thus they assist Heaven and Earth in perpetuating all things and people.
The Lord of Mount Heng presides over the celestial officials;
he wears a robe of vermilion radiance and a crown of ninefold cinnabar solar essence.
He wears the seal of the True One of Night-Light and rides a red dragon;
the deity of the mountain peak has the surname Chong.
The Realized Person Xu of the讳 (Hui) lineage said:
"The summit of Mount Rong contains the sweet springs and divine waters of Kunchi to the southwest;
by drinking them, one attains longevity and ascends to immortality."
As for the wine of Mount Jun and the stone fungi of Mount Song,
in the past the practitioner Hupiaozhi lived in seclusion within the Stone Chamber of Sunset Peak.
By drinking from it, one attains the Way.
The stream is called Xiayang (Twilight).
The height of the mountain above the stream is nine thousand seven hundred and thirty *zhang*.
At the summit of the highest peak to the north of all the mountains,
one looks down upon the myriad hills as if they were mere anthills;
even peaks such as Ziga and Yunmi cannot compare to it.
Thus, Lu Zai wrote a couplet in a poem:
"From five thousand li away, it can be seen from afar;
among seventy-two peaks, it is the highest."
To the south is the Temple of Zhurong;
its foundations remain there.
Formerly, there was Guangtian Guan (Light Heaven Monastery) located there.
According to the *Fudi zhi* (Record of Blessed Lands),
this is the blessed land of the Twenty-second Gāntán (Light Altar).
To the east is Xī'ān (Cottage of Rest).
This was the place where Master Baiyun invited Master He to inquire about the Way.
There is also the Shangqing Courtyard,
situated by the cliffs where the walls were carved into the rock to dwell upon the precipice.
In the past, there was a recluse known as Lanweng (the Lazy Old Man).
He subsisted solely on swallowing talismans and drinking tea;
he appeared and disappeared without constancy.
At the end of the Jianlong era, one entered Mount Hua from the west;
there lies the Azure Jade Altar (Qingyutan), which belongs to the Twenty-one Blessed Lands (Fudi).
Thus, a poem in a single quatrain from the *Dongyuan Ji Fudi Zhi* says:
The Jade Altar faces Mount Shou,
its lofty peaks appearing as if they might forever press down upon the giant turtle.
It was here that the Perfected Men once dwelt in seclusion.
He personally planted the green, coiled peaches before the cave.
In the past, during the time of King Ling of Chu, the summit of [Ling]rong collapsed,
and he obtained the "Diagram of the Nine-Headed Human Sovereign."
According to the *Tu jing* (Atlas of Scriptures),
atop the Qingyu Altar is the place where the Immortals practiced the Way;
it rises in solitary isolation, traversing perilous heights to reach the summit.
When the state completes the Golden Register Retreat (Jinlu Zhai),
the golden dragons and jade tablets are likewise stored in this place.
Furthermore, the *Yuetu Jing* states:
Below there is the volcanic *zhī* fungus.
The *Shennong Bencao* states:
"The red *zhī* grows on Mount Heng; the red *zhī* is precisely the volcanic *zhī*."
At night, there is a spiritual light like a flying candle;
the common people call it the "sacred lamp.
The *Caoyi tu* states:
Mount Heng possesses nine kinds of divine fungi (*zhī*).
Three stalks grow filling the valley to the east of Lotus Peak;
three stalks grow beneath this altar.
The three original gold tablets are located to the east of Jinjian Peak.
Furthermore, the *Dili zhi* (Records of Geography) states:
"Mount Heng has two altars, Qingyu and Baiyi; Qingyu is the Immortal’s Bridge."
The "White Jade" (Báibì) is the Radiant Celestial Altar (Guāngtiāntán); it is located atop the peak of this mountain, piercing through like the form of celestial immortals or golden characters.
Its surface is several feet wide, much like the Golden Court (Jīntíng) of Tóngbǎi and the Golden Altar (Jīntán) of Jūqū.
During the Sui dynasty, Guan was changed to Si;
this is the present-day Shangfeng Monastery.
As for the local deity of the monastery grounds:
This is the true sanctuary of the Daoist observatory and the land of the local deities;
when the temple monks ceased their offerings of incense and lamps,
the springs that supplied the temple immediately dried up.
The Śākya clan further renamed the Jade Terrace of Green Jasper the "Arahant’s Path-Walking Terrace," which is this very place.
There is also a *xianli* (immortal pear) tree;
the *Xiangzhong ji* states:
To the east of Mount Zhurong there is a divine pear,
as large as a peck-measure and red as the sun, resembling the fruit of the *ping*.
It is also like the peonies of Qingcheng, the lotuses of Mount Taibai, and the *longnü* bamboo of Mount Luofu.
There is also stone marrow;
formerly, Pan Jue, the Magistrate of Hengyang, beheld it.
Cracks appeared in the stone, from which purple mud emerged.
A sutra states:
"It is named 'Emergence'; it opens once every five hundred years, and when it does, [the mud] flows forth."
If a person obtains it and eats it, they can ascend lightly into the air during the daytime.
There is also the "dragon-pine," which sometimes transforms into a great python.
It charms people but does not cause them harm.
The pine trees that sweep the altar are called "dwarf trees" or "ten-thousand-year pines";
they do not exceed one zhang in height.
Its roots were lush and verdant;
its strange form resembled a dragon. It was, then, as follows:
Our Emperor’s longevity is like that of the pine trees here.

Furthermore, there are the Tiger-Run Spring, the Sunset Brook, and the Guest-of-the-Sun Pavilion from which one may view the rising sun; the Dragon King Hall, the Stabilizing-Mind Rock, the Needle-Holding Cliff, the Most Victorious Cliff, and the Night-Light Cliff, where many mountain goblins dwell; as well as the Thunder Pond and the Wind Abyss Cave.
Whenever rain is about to fall, a fierce wind howls, emanating from its cave.
Thus, Tao Bi of our own dynasty composed a quatrain titled "Ascending Mount Rong," which says:
"I have once reached the solitary summit of Mount Zhurong."
I follow the bright moon on foot to lodge at the Chan gate;
Deep in the night, a sudden downpour strikes the window.
Lying down, I listen to the wind and thunder halfway up the mountain.
Mount Zigai (Purple Canopy Peak) rises over five thousand four hundred *zhang*.
It has the appearance of being enveloped by purple mists and flowers;
its shape is like a canopy.
It is also called Huagai Peak (Flower Canopy Peak).
Furthermore, it is said that Xiaozigai (Little Purple Canopy) is Huagai Peak.
All the other peaks face Zhurong as if in a gesture of respectful salutation.
Only this peak faces south;
this is because it is the source of the Zhuling (Cinnabar Peak) Celestial Cavern, facing southward.
Mount Zhurong is assigned to the virtue of Fire.
Although it is the most honored among the five peaks,
it possesses two blessed lands (fudi)— Qingyu and Baiyi—
where the offices of terrestrial immortals are administered; thus, it is appropriate that it be ranked below a celestial grotto (dongtian).
Furthermore, its topographical formation is clearly oriented toward the south.
Thus, in his poem "Gazing at Mount [Tai]" (Wàng Yuè), the Tang poet Du Fú wrote, in brief:
"The Five Peaks of Zhurong are most venerable."
Peak follows peak in alternating rise and fall;
Mount Zigai alone does not face [the central peak].
This is what is meant by "vying for primacy as they gaze at one another from their towering heights."
The *Xiangzhong ji* states:
whenever the weather is clear and bright,
a pair of cranes circles and soars above it.
Now there are the Crane-Crying Terrace, the Immortal Tea Hearth, the White Crane Spring, and the Precious Dew Terrace.
Here, beneath this terrace, Xia Yu buried a jar of precious dew,
which contained within it purple-gold jade-essence.
If a person consumes it, they will attain longevity.
Furthermore, the *Fangyu ji* states that there is a Pool of the Immortals at the summit of the peak.
The cranes and egrets cry out at night, sounding like the turning of the watch-sticks.
To the east is the Tianbao Terrace;
to the west is the Zigai Courtyard.
In ancient times, this was the place where Fu Daxian attained the Way;
furthermore, Tan Qiao refined his elixir here,
and the venerable Master Chen Zangqi also resided there.
Ginkgo trees are planted extensively there.
Below the tea gardens lies the Wang Family Medicine Hall,
situated at Cui Lu Rock.
He had long taken mountain celery and howu (he-shou-wu) and reached over one hundred and twenty years of age;
later, he moved to the foot of Yonghe Peak.
This is where the elixir for cultivating the spirit was refined at the Night-Music Spring in the Spirit-Ridge Stream.
Yunmibong Peak rises over five thousand three hundred *zhang*;
south of it lies Yunpungsa Temple.
To the west is Dayu Rock,
where King Yu of antiquity once performed purification rites and prayed for the Perfected One.
There is also the stone chamber of the Immortal Danhuo.
To the northwest of the peak,
whenever it is a dark and cloudy night,
celestial lamps appear.
It leaps like a flying candle.
Some say that in the past,
Lord Ziyang of the Zhou dynasty once stored his elixir here in a pit.
To the northwest lies Yinzhenping;
atop it stands the Huixiantan altar,
situated amidst a cluster of jagged peaks.
Level and even, it encircles five or seven *li*.
It is a celestial cave and a blessed land.
The various deities who oversee the realm all compare their merits at this place of leisure and repose;
auspicious clouds constantly cover it.
On the midpoint of the peak is the Stele of Yu.
When King Yu arrived here,
he measured the height at four thousand ten *zhang*;
all [the inscriptions] were in the script of the *guikou* (tortoises and dragons).

In the past, there was a woodcutter who saw two dragons entwined upon a stone wall atop a stele; their twin eyes flashed like lightning, and the surface of the stone was so brilliantly polished that one could not look directly at them.
Terrified, he fled without ceasing;
thereafter, there was no one to be seen at all.
It was like the Golden and Silver Bridges of Tiantai or the Jade Beam of Beiyue.
Ancient and modern are seen as one and the same.
Bi Tian composed a quatrain on the Stele of Yu, which says:
"The work of flood control accomplished, the kingly enterprise flourished."
Excellent counsel bestowed upon the world is plain and clear;
yet even when engraved in refined script, the *yan* and *jiakou* characters remain difficult to discern—
how much more so when hidden deep within the clouds, never revealed?
Furthermore, there were fine trees with interlacing branches and fragrant grasses with continuous stems;
yellow birds and white monkeys produced diverse sounds that shared a single rhythm.
To the north lies the Flowing Continent (Sāṭhāgata-dvīpa), on whose shores there are couches and seats made of white jade.
Beneath these couches is a spring of jade sand,
the color of vermilion.
By drinking it, one ascends to heaven.
To the west lies Peach Blossom Spring,
which was visited by the itinerant monk Huiguang.
Seeing the peach blossoms in full bloom,
he plucked several branches and went out.
Everyone marveled at this.
He led his companion back to visit again,
but found nothing at all.
Shilin Peak (石廩峰) is over four thousand five hundred *zhang* high.
The *Xiangzhong ji* states:
"Its peak rises loftily;
viewed from afar, it has the shape of a granary."
There are stone statues standing on both sides of the gate;
whenever there is a violent wind, thunder, or rain,
the people living at the foot of the mountain hear the sound of the stone gate closing.
The tradition states that this is the convenient gate to the cave-heaven of Zhuling.
During the Jin dynasty, Mao Jing served as the Magistrate of Hengyang.
The Man people petitioned him, saying,
"The storehouses are all full of honey."
The scene was solemn and reverent;
he prayed with devotion and went in person to look, whereupon he indeed saw it.
He then prostrated himself and took it.
There is also the Stone of Leftover Grain,
which was transformed from the provisions left behind by King Yu in ancient times. He used these provisions to ascend as an immortal.
Furthermore, a Daoist from Nanyang traveled to this mountain;
having ascended a precipitous valley—some say he filled the entire valley—he did not emerge.
This occurred during the Zhihe era of the Northern Zhou dynasty.
There was a man of the Way named Li Hunrong who gathered fuling at this site; by ingesting it,
he attained immortality.
Furthermore, the *Jingzhou ji* states:
"It is also known as Shiquǐn (Stone Granary).
Within the stone chamber, the sound of reciting the scriptures is often heard."
It is further stated:
"Seokkun Peak lies to the east of Mangok;
it is called the Lesser Stone Granary."
The *Fangyu ji* states:
"Its shape is like that of a granary;
it has two doors."
It opens and closes;
when it closes, it also has the form of a lock and key.
Furthermore, the *Xiangzhong ji* states:
If it is opened, the year will be one of scarcity;
if it is closed, the year will be one of abundance.
As the Record says:
Formerly, Liu Yimin traveled to Mount Heng and reached a secluded valley.
From afar he saw two rocks,
separated by water, which prevented him from crossing.
He encountered an old man again who said,
"In the stone granary east of Xiayang Ferry, there are all the elixirs and superior medicines of the immortals.
Liu went there once more, but he became lost on the way and did not reach it again.
For this reason, it is called the "Ferry of Delusion.
Thus, the poem on Mount Bitian Shilin Peak says in brief:
"I hear the opening and closing of the seasonal rains."
In the autumn of that year, one perceives both scarcity and abundance.
It is also said:
"The four seasons bring new and old snow."
Opening and closing the winds of a single day—
how could the supreme medicine ever be obtained?
This refers to those for whom the path through the mazes of delusion rarely becomes passable.
Above is the Yuqing Guan (Jade Purity Abbey).
On its summit are the Refining Elixir Terrace of Immortal Chen, the Stone Planted by Ghosts, the Thunder Pool, the Wind Cavern, the Scripture Recitation Altar, and the Bathing Elixir Spring.
To the southeast is the site of Taiching Guan;
to the west is the site of Dongyang Gong;
and directly to the east is the site of Taichu Guan.
Tianzhu Peak is over four thousand eighty *zhang* in height.
Its form resembles a pair of pillars;
both its upper and lower ends rise steeply for a hundred *zhang*.
The *Jiuyuzhi* states:
"Among the three hundred and sixty famous mountains, there are eight pillars;
this is the sixth."
At the foot of the mountain is Tiantzhusi Temple.
To the northwest of the mountain is a stone chamber.
During the Tahe era of the Wu dynasty.
A rustic man named Li Dongyan, an old hermit, dwells there.
He says of himself:
"In the past, Lady Wei planted fragrant white vetiver on this mountain."
If a person prepares and consumes Acorus calamus (xiangpu),
they may attain a lifespan equal to that of Heaven and Earth.
However, whether a method is great or small, it is attained by those who possess sincerity and faith.
I have come and gone here for over fifty years.
I am now one hundred and seventeen years old.
It has been less than two months since I went to Qingcheng late in life.
At night, he gazed toward his dwelling place as flames soared into the sky; at dawn,
people from the foot of the mountain went there to observe it.
It was completely empty of anything.
To the north were the foundations of a hermitage and a stone cave,
where one saw only tangled grass and cold ashes.
At that time, there was also a practitioner of the Way who was gathering medicinal herbs on a remote peak;
he had no idea where they resided.
Long ago, Chen Xingming of the Western Jin dynasty encountered two divine beings.
He preached the Way atop this peak.
Beyond the five peaks,
there are sixty-seven other peaks.
Although these sacred sites are inferior to those of the Five Peaks,
they too possess features worthy of observation;
they are now each categorized according to their affiliation with the Five Peaks.
The sequence is recorded in detail below.
It is named after the Five Peaks to which Zhurong is assigned.
To the east of Cedao Peak (Side-dao Peak) is a stone chamber.
This was the place where Huichizi practiced his cultivation.
During the Three Kingdoms period,
Li Yiqi encountered him there.
Yet they are able to conceal their forms and hide their shadows,
and can foreknow the fortunes and misfortunes of others by means of the principles of yin and yang and the calculation of numbers.
Furthermore, there was Xue Youqi’s Altar for Paying Homage to the Dipper (Lidoutan).
Around the perimeter of the altar grew "scale-scaled" grass (chilincao),
also known as the "Jade Lamp Stand" (Yudengtai).
Its leaves are layered one upon another;
the roots are purple and the sap is red.
They resemble apricot leaves but are soft.
It cannot be found by searching for it.
Fire is prohibited; it should be ground into powder using iron vessels.
When taken by people, there is no deficiency [in its efficacy].
One must abstain from the five pungent roots, blood, meat, and their like for three years,
thereby communicating with the divine, prolonging life,
and attaining immortality. Furthermore, one can dry mercury so that it instantly becomes "horse-tooth" mercury, which constitutes a true treasure.
In the past, Tan Qiao often gathered this [herb] and took a *fūncùn* spoonful to assist his internal medicines.
Later, he attained transformation while on Mount Shu.
As for Huiri Peak (*Huìrì fēng*), in ancient times a high monk first rested here.
Later, by imperial decree of the Sui Emperor, he went to the Huiri Monastery (Huiri Daochang).
Furthermore, the eminent monk of the Tang dynasty resided for a long time at Mili Hermitage,
where they discussed the scriptures and teachings.
He was profoundly learned and possessed vast eloquence;
he was a preeminent lineage among those who took refuge [in the Triple Gem].
He himself composed the *Biographies of the Eighteen Eminent Monks*.
Later, he traveled to the imperial court and was granted the honorary title "Beneficent Sun" (Huìrì) by imperial decree.
What was formerly called Qinren Peak (Qín rén fēng),
his disciples subsequently changed its name to Huìrì Peak.
Biluo Peak stands as a neighbor to mist and clouds;
looking down, it overlooks Daming Temple and lies directly upon the main road to You Mountain.
Guanyin Rock and the Yuyang Stūpa are both situated below it; from here,
one looks down upon the southern part of Mount Yue.
The view extends for a thousand *li*.
To the south of Yeonhamaeong Peak lies Daemyeongsa Temple;
behind it are Daemyeongtap Pagoda and Ramgoryan Cliff.
In front lies the Altar of the Path (Xingdao Tan).
To the east are the Enduring Chamber of Li Yuehou and the Laziness Cavern (Lanzan Yan); these five peaks above are subordinate to Mount Zhurong.
The Altar of the Twenty-seven Peaks subordinate to Mount Zigai, as well as Huangdi Yan and Huangle Dong, are the sites where the petitions of the Three Heavens were presented.
To the east is Dayu Rock.
King Yu performed a purification rite there and dreamed that a messenger from the Azure Waters brought him a divine lord from the South, who bestowed upon him a golden tablet and a jade book;
it was for this reason that the site was named.
In the area of Nüyouduan, there is the Shiyuan Yinzhenping.
To the southwest, at the source of the stream,
there is a rock several *zhang* high and several *zhang* wide, which is split down the middle.
Upon that stone cliff, there are carved characters which read:
"The water of the Jade Sand is as sweet and fragrant as milk."
If a person gets but a single sip,
they will endure as long as earth and heaven.
Or, when a person arrives here—
I heard only the sound of water beneath the rocks;
listening to the left, it was immediately on the right, and listening to the right, it was immediately on the left.
The record states:
"If one seeks out the source of the water,
there is a pear tree."
He struck the tree with a stone,
and the immortal emerged from within.
An ancient worthy once composed a single quatrain titled "The Source of the Broken Stone":
A single draught of vermilion blossoms sustains ten thousand years;
travelers vie to visit, hearing only the sound.
Who would have known that this well had long been buried in sand?
He was still able to preserve his entire family’s lives for several lifetimes.
To the east lies the Immortal’s Furnace Rock, where cinnabar flows;
upon its cliffs grows coral-like fungi.
On dark and cloudy nights, a spiritual light appears;
the common people call it the "Holy Lamp," and it is also known as the "Terrace of Radiance."
At Huixian Peak, Xue Youqi once annotated the *Lingbao Jing*. There he encountered the two sages Bianbai and Xiansheng,
with whom he discussed the profound mysteries and expounded upon the wondrous art of the five true spirits and the wandering of the soul.
Suddenly, a fragrant wind circled the assembly,
and auspicious vapors coalesced like mist;
then, the two ascended the western platform.
He was seen dimly, like a crimson figure, riding through the air;
as he gazed upon him in worship,
he suddenly vanished from sight.
The smoke then dispersed.
Below was the Hall of Master Bailing (Baibyun Seonsaeng).
Regarding the Descent-of-Truth Peak (Gwangjŏn Pong), the *Seon nok* (Records of the Immortals) states:
In the past, the Princess of Yan Di performed purification rites and prayed to the True One.
Moved by her devotion, the Mysterious Lord descended to transmit the Way to her.
Several years later, she transformed her physical form and refined her bones, ascending together with him.
Beneath the Peak of Immortal Rock (Seonyeom-bong) is a stone cavern,
lofty and spacious enough to accommodate one or two hundred people.
In the past, Master Liu Gen practiced the Way of Di-yi (Unity with the Sovereign) here, refining his spirit and paying homage to the Dipper.
To the east is the altar for spirit-summoning rites;
the lamps, ritual implements, and incense burners are fashioned from stone.

Pingwei Liang, Pingwei Liang.

Master Lü Zhi-zhen. It is unknown where he was from.

The Master then traveled eastward for over ten li until he reached a thatched cottage; seeing a man by the fence with chickens and dogs, his appearance was like that of a farmer.

Take it from the mind.

However, as his bones had not yet been formed,

It was over a chi in length and sweet in flavor.

When he lifted his head from the water, it suddenly vanished.

He was even better than when he had arrived.
Furthermore, the assembly of Daoist practitioners at the Xian Guan (Immortal Abbey) were startled and marveled, saying,

"Why has it been so long? There is no place to stay in the mountains.
The Master, startled by this, said to himself:

One night had already passed and more than a month had elapsed.

Having met with the Immortal Cai and his son, [the narrative continues].

Now that I have also fortunately become your mother,"

I knew that you had once traveled to Mount Nanyue.
I have just been commissioned by the Lord of Donghua to serve as a terrestrial immortal of the Yusi Mountains,

Master Dao has already been penetrating the profound source for fifty years.

none of us dare go down the mountain.

"Do not touch my trigger."
He also said to his two sons,
"The foot of the mountain is still far away and the tiger is already rampaging.
Why do you not come up this palisade for now?"
The two sons trembled with fear;
they then climbed up by grasping the branches,
intending to reach the human settlement before nightfall.
Suddenly, thirty or fifty people passed by—
some monks, some Daoists, some men, and some women.
The singers and dancers suddenly arrived at the place where the bow was kept.
The crowd became enraged and said:
"This morning, two bandits already killed my Chan monk;
I am currently in pursuit of them.
Next, who dares to oppose my General?"
He then revealed his true identity and departed.
Both sons heard his words and subsequently interrogated the hunter, saying:
"This is a *chāng* ghost, one who was devoured by a tiger;
he merely acts as a guide for tigers.
The two sons then questioned the hunter regarding his surname and name.
He replied, "The one who advanced his name was Niu.
The two sons were greatly delighted and said,
"The second line of the poem concerning the earthen figurines has now been proven true."
"Niu Jin" is simply "Tejin" (Special Advance).
"Jiangjun" is simply "Hu" (Tiger).
He then urged the hunters [to pursue him].
He readjusted his arrow;
the hunter lit it, and he had barely retreated to the palisade when it struck.
Suddenly, a tiger roared as it approached;
its front paw struck the trigger,
and the arrow struck its third stripe, piercing its heart so that it collapsed, struggling for a moment before dying.
The various wandering ghosts fled and turned back;
prostrating themselves before the tiger, they wept most piteously, saying,
"Who else has slain our General?"
The two sons, provoked by anger, rebuked them, saying:
"You ignorant, lowly ghosts!
You were bitten by tigers while alive, and now you die."
I am now here to take revenge for you;
unable to feel shame or offer an apology,
I still dare to wail aloud in grief.
"How can there be a ghost so devoid of spiritual power as this? he said, and then fell silent.
Suddenly, a ghost replied, "I had no idea you were the General;
it was only upon hearing your words, young sir, that I realized my error in great terror. He then stepped onto the tiger's tail and reviled him.
He thanked him and departed.

He then explained the matter to his two sons, gave them one *hu* of white silver, and sent them back with the hunter. This account appears in the *Chuanqi* (Tales of the Strange) under the entry for Xiang Ziwen.
Xiang was a native of Changsha.
During the Baoli era,
he obtained an official post in Hengzhou;
being poor, he was unable to return home.
Delighting in the splendors of mountains and waters,
he once visited the Temple of the God of the Peak during the height of summer.
He stayed for over ten days.
Suddenly, there appeared a man wearing a blue turban and a purple fur robe.

his beard and eyebrows were as if painted.

When questioned, he replied,
"I am Gong Qingzhang. My family has been established in Luoyang for generations."
In his youth, he encountered Sima Yinyuan at the foot of Mount Minggao.
Yinyuan was a spiritual official of the Weiyu Cavern-Heaven (*dongtian*).
Regarding all the five sacred peaks, the four great rivers, and the cavern-heavens and blessed lands:

who weighs merits and offenses and investigates good and evil.
I heard from the Office of the Nine Heavenly Messengers that Ingen had said to Keichō:

Consequently, he attained deliverance from the world.

Ziwen performed it with great devotion.
Qingchang looked at his attendants, had a zither brought out, and played upon it.

The resonance was clear and far-reaching;
it was no ordinary sound.
We accompanied him for several consecutive days.

Qingchang replied:
"It is not yet possible.
You should enter official service.
We shall meet again at Mount Zhongtiao in eighteen years."
Ziwen bowed twice and requested words of instruction.
Qingchang said, "Learning precedes action;
when one encounters the right time and achieves their ambitions."
"You should exert yourself in this;
as for practices such as breath control and the ingestion of medicinal elixirs,
these are merely secondary matters."
Shiwen entreated him earnestly three times.
Keichō replied,
"I shall await our next meeting."
Ziwen said, "There are further instructions and admonitions;
I vow to receive and follow them."
Keichō reflected for a long time and said,
"Your ancestors' coffins have been interred temporarily in a monastery; they are suffering greatly from being conscripted as laborers by spirits."
He early selected an auspicious site to conclude the great affair.
Ziwen shed tears, bowed in thanks,
and departed with graceful ease.
Master Nian Shaoyuan was naturally inclined toward poetry, the Classics,
and the writings of Laozi, Zhuangzi, Wenzi, and Liezi from his youth.
One day he went to Jinling;

The palace and its precincts were solemn and grave.

who, leaning upon a desk, addressed Shaoyuan, saying:

You may open the registers yourself.
The register says:"
Nie Shaoyuan entered the Way at the age of eighteen.
At twenty, he received the complete teachings of Shangqing.
At twenty-two, he went to Mount Nanyue.
He then closed the scroll and remained in contemplation for a long time.
Later, returning from Jinling, he went to Weningshan.
He built a dwelling to live in,
remaining aloof from worldly conventions,
and styled himself the "Nameless One."
The world for the most part addressed him as a "Master of Refinement" (Lian Shi).
He served his mother with utmost diligence and toil.
One day, rising at dawn, he bathed and said:
My great-uncle Jie said:
"In every generation of our family, it is fitting that we cultivate and refine ourselves;
let us be diligent and never forget the teachings of the Most High."
Suddenly, four cranes gathered upon the roof,
and a divine light descended from the sky;
those who saw it from afar mistook it for a fire.
Upon approaching him, he was found to have vanished without a trace;
it was simply that Shao Yuan had already passed away.
The four cranes and the divine light also drifted away into the distance.
At dawn the next day, a servant from the Zhuang household came to report:
"The Master of Refinement (Lian-shi) and three Daoist priests, dressed in crimson and green, were riding;
they were followed by several attendants."
He donned his cap and belt and departed toward the south.
The Master of Refinement turned his head and said,
"I am going to Mount Nanyue."
Pan Fa, style name Wenbo, was a native of Longyou.
From childhood, he received the transmission of the dharma registers;
he issued summonses to spirits and deities,
practiced talismans, and dispensed medicine.
He relieved the suffering of the sick,
and his reputation spread far and wide.
On the night of the Yuanjie Festival, he entered a state of meditative stillness and addressed the True Official of Nanyue, saying:
Yesterday was the day of the winter solstice (Lajiri).
The neighbor to the east reported that the invocation of the Eastern Peak had already been successfully performed for his deliverance,
but it remains uncertain whether the invocation of the Southern Peak for his rebirth has been accomplished.
The Eastern Peak governs the collection of souls and the examination of transgressions;
the Southern Peak conducts the refinement and salvation;
what, then, does the Lord of the Dharma preside over?
The True Official’s Dream states:
"Regarding the divisions of the five sacred peaks, their respective regions and fields,
as well as the celestial grottoes and blessed lands."
The famous mountains, streams, and valleys each have their presiding deities;
they oversee the merits and transgressions of humanity,
as well as the nation’s revenues, resources, and implements.
Furthermore, it is said that all species of water and land,
those of the fiery mountains and the four great rivers, and the class of quadrupeds that carry burdens,
[are likewise included].
"On Mount Nanyue there is a barefoot immortal;
if you cultivate virtue with diligence,
you will surely encounter him."
He was actually the master of Zi (Zi-shi), namely Li Shouwei.
Quoted from the *Beimeng suozuan* by the Daoist Qin Baoyan: "Qin Baoyan was diligent in his ascetic practices."
Once, he addressed the True Lord of Nanyue, saying, "Why does the High True Lord require paper money? There is something I do not yet understand.
Shortly thereafter, he dreamed at night that the True Lord said to him:
"Paper money is merely what the netherworld officials record;
what need have I for it?
At this, his faith in Mount [Yue] increased all the more.
Ma Xisheng of Hunan succeeded to his father’s position.
For several consecutive years,
